_note: Narration script for the Pain management module (CPP-013-AO v7.2, CTL-097, CPPRO-013). Lee voice on eleven_v4, one take, short conversational sentences. The prompt sent to ElevenLabs starts with the [calmly] tag and spells EOC as "E O C", IN as "intranasal", MAD as "mad", and microg as "micrograms"; captions use the text here.

lines.head: Introduction
sentences: Pain management.
What every Ambulance Officer needs to know.

lines.head: A human right
sentences: Pain relief is a fundamental human right.
Start it as soon as it's clinically appropriate.
And don't rely only on medicines.
Reassurance, distraction, splinting and posture all help.
The aim is a comfortable, tolerable level. Not zero.

lines.head: Assess
sentences: Get a pain score before and after every treatment.
If they can talk, let them rate it.
If they can't, use a behavioural tool. FLACC for little ones. PAINAD for advanced dementia.
And watch the trend.

lines.head: Multimodal
sentences: Still in pain? Think multimodal.
Paracetamol, 1000 milligrams, if none in the last 4 hours.
Ibuprofen, 400 milligrams, if no anti-inflammatories in the last 6 hours.
Any doubt about ibuprofen? Don't give it.
And methoxyflurane, 3 mils, repeated once.

lines.head: IN fentanyl
sentences: Authorised to carry IN fentanyl?
Consult the EOC Clinician first.
The patient needs uncontrolled or severe pain, and a sedation score under 2.
Adults need a systolic of 100 or more.
For children, the EOC Clinician advises the dose.

lines.head: The sedation score
sentences: Nought is awake and alert.
1 is easy to rouse.
2 is easy to rouse, but they can't stay awake.
3 is hard to rouse.
Hit 2, or the blood pressure drops below the limit? Stop the fentanyl, and call the EOC Clinician.

lines.head: Giving it
sentences: Use a 1 mil luer-lock syringe and a MAD.
Prime it so what's left is the dose.
Aim up and out, toward the top of the ear.
Over 0.3 mils? Split it between the nostrils.
Then obs every 5 minutes, and keep checking that sedation score.

lines.head: Ketamine
sentences: Some crews also carry ketamine wafers.
Pain 7 to 10, a normal GCS, and aged 16 to 64.
One 25 milligram wafer under the tongue. You can repeat it once after 15 minutes.
Not for psychiatric presentations.

lines.head: Stay safe
sentences: Opioids can slow breathing.
If breathing gets ineffective, support it with the bag.
And the EOC Clinician may advise naloxone.
Lowest effective dose, every time.
